Appendix A Additional Variational Derivations

Figure 3 illustrates the gradient-grouping preference underlying the following fixed-observation derivations.

A.1 Stationary Gibbs form

The following is the formal statement summarized in Section 3.

Proposition A.1 (Stationary Gibbs form).

Fix τ>0\tau>0. If P⋆P^{\star} is an interior stationary point of ℒτ,ϵ​(⋅,W)\mathcal{L}_{\tau,\epsilon}(\cdot;W) over 𝒫M,K\mathcal{P}_{M,K}, then for every routed item mm,

pm​k⋆=exp⁡(sm​k​(P⋆)/τ)∑ℓ=1Kexp⁡(sm​ℓ​(P⋆)/τ),sm​k​(P):=2​⟨Gk,g~m⟩dk​(P)+ϵ−‖Gk‖2(dk​(P)+ϵ)2.p^{\star}_{mk}=\frac{\exp\!\big(s_{mk}(P^{\star})/\tau\big)}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\exp\!\big(s_{m\ell}(P^{\star})/\tau\big)},\qquad s_{mk}(P):=\frac{2\left\langle G_{k},\tilde{g}_{m}\right\rangle}{d_{k}(P)+\epsilon}-\frac{\left\lVert G_{k}\right\rVert^{2}}{(d_{k}(P)+\epsilon)^{2}}. (4)
Proof.

By Proposition 3.1,

ℒτ,ϵ(P;W)=−∑k=1K‖Gk‖2dk​(P)+ϵ+τ∑m=1M∑k=1Kpm​klogpm​k.\mathcal{L}_{\tau,\epsilon}(P;W)=-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\left\lVert G_{k}\right\rVert^{2}}{d_{k}(P)+\epsilon}+\tau\sum_{m=1}^{M}\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{mk}\log p_{mk}.

Differentiating with respect to pm​kp_{mk} gives

∂ℒτ,ϵ∂pm​k=−(2​⟨Gk,g~m⟩dk​(P)+ϵ−‖Gk‖2(dk​(P)+ϵ)2)+τ⁡(1+log⁡pm​k).\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\tau,\epsilon}}{\partial p_{mk}}=-\left(\frac{2\left\langle G_{k},\tilde{g}_{m}\right\rangle}{d_{k}(P)+\epsilon}-\frac{\left\lVert G_{k}\right\rVert^{2}}{(d_{k}(P)+\epsilon)^{2}}\right)+\tau(1+\log p_{mk}). (5)

Introducing a Lagrange multiplier αm\alpha_{m} for the row constraint ∑k=1Kpm​k=1\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{mk}=1, the stationarity condition is

∂ℒτ,ϵ∂pm​k+αm=0.\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\tau,\epsilon}}{\partial p_{mk}}+\alpha_{m}=0.

Substituting (5), rearranging, and normalizing over kk yields (4). ∎

Appendix B Optimization geometry, Clustering structure, and Spectral view

B.1 Proof of Proposition 4.1

For fixed gradient observations under hard assignments, each sample mm is assigned to exactly one expert, forming clusters 𝒞k={m:pm​k=1}\mathcal{C}_{k}=\{m:p_{mk}=1\}.

The surrogate aggregate of observations assigned to expert kk is:

Gk=∑m∈𝒞kg~m.G_{k}=\sum_{m\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\tilde{g}_{m}.

Its squared norm expands as:

‖Gk‖2=∑i,j∈𝒞k⟨g~i,g~j⟩.\|G_{k}\|^{2}=\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\langle\tilde{g}_{i},\tilde{g}_{j}\rangle.

Therefore, the objective

∑k‖Gk‖2|𝒞k|+ϵ=∑k1|𝒞k|+ϵ​∑i,j∈𝒞k⟨g~i,g~j⟩\sum_{k}\frac{\|G_{k}\|^{2}}{|\mathcal{C}_{k}|+\epsilon}=\sum_{k}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{k}|+\epsilon}\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\langle\tilde{g}_{i},\tilde{g}_{j}\rangle

is a load-normalized association within each observation cluster. Maximizing it rewards positive co-routing affinity and discourages cancellation within the surrogate aggregates. ∎

Self-association and cross-observation agreement.

For general soft assignments, the full Gram reward decomposes as

𝒜ϵ​(P,W)=∑k∑mpm​k2​‖g~m‖2+∑i≠jpi​k​pj​k​⟨g~i,g~j⟩dk​(P)+ϵ.\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}(P;W)=\sum_{k}\frac{\sum_{m}p_{mk}^{2}\|\tilde{g}_{m}\|^{2}+\sum_{i\neq j}p_{ik}p_{jk}\langle\tilde{g}_{i},\tilde{g}_{j}\rangle}{d_{k}(P)+\epsilon}.

The first term retains observation self-association; the second scores agreement between distinct observations. The diagonal can favor concentrated assignments even when the off-diagonal associations vanish. For example, with M=K=2M=K=2 and W=I2W=I_{2}, the uniform assignment has reward 1/(1+ϵ)1/(1+\epsilon), whereas P=I2P=I_{2} has reward 2/(1+ϵ)2/(1+\epsilon). The full Gram choice underlies the Euclidean aggregate identity and the k-means characterization below; removing its diagonal defines a different objective. The experiments evaluate the full-Gram criterion.

B.2 Hard-Routing Restriction and k-Means Equivalence

We now restrict the variational free energy to hard assignment matrices

ℋM,K:={P∈{0,1}M×K|P​𝟏K=𝟏M}⊂𝒫M,K.\mathcal{H}_{M,K}:=\left\{P\in\{0,1\}^{M\times K}\;\middle|\;P\mathbf{1}_{K}=\mathbf{1}_{M}\right\}\subset\mathcal{P}_{M,K}.

Under P∈ℋM,KP\in\mathcal{H}_{M,K}, each routed item is assigned to exactly one expert. For the discrete equivalence below we set ϵ=0\epsilon=0 and restrict to nonempty clusters, matching the usual k-means convention; the stabilizer only handles numerical empty-cluster cases.

Theorem B.1 (Hard-routing restriction = k-means).

Under the Euclidean gradient-Gram affinity

Wi​j=⟨g~i,g~j⟩,W_{ij}=\left\langle\tilde{g}_{i},\tilde{g}_{j}\right\rangle,

minimizing ℒ0,0​(P,W)\mathcal{L}_{0,0}(P;W) over nonempty hard clusters is equivalent to minimizing the classical k-means objective on {g~m}m=1M\{\tilde{g}_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M}.

Proof.

Let {g~m}m=1M⊂ℝd\{\tilde{g}_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be the detached gradient observations and assume hard routing

pm​k∈{0,1},𝒞k={m∣pm​k=1}.p_{mk}\in\{0,1\},\qquad\mathcal{C}_{k}=\{m\mid p_{mk}=1\}.

Let |𝒞k||\mathcal{C}_{k}| denote cluster size. Classical k-means minimizes

𝒥k​-means=∑k=1K∑m∈𝒞k‖g~m−μk‖2,μk=1|𝒞k|​∑m∈𝒞kg~m.\mathcal{J}_{k\text{-means}}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\left\lVert\tilde{g}_{m}-\mu_{k}\right\rVert^{2},\qquad\mu_{k}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{k}|}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\tilde{g}_{m}.

Expanding,

‖g~m−μk‖2=‖g~m‖2−2​⟨g~m,μk⟩+‖μk‖2.\left\lVert\tilde{g}_{m}-\mu_{k}\right\rVert^{2}=\left\lVert\tilde{g}_{m}\right\rVert^{2}-2\left\langle\tilde{g}_{m},\mu_{k}\right\rangle+\left\lVert\mu_{k}\right\rVert^{2}.

Summing over m∈𝒞km\in\mathcal{C}_{k} and substituting μk\mu_{k} yields

∑m∈𝒞k‖g~m−μk‖2=∑m∈𝒞k‖g~m‖2−1|𝒞k|​‖∑m∈𝒞kg~m‖2.\sum_{m\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\left\lVert\tilde{g}_{m}-\mu_{k}\right\rVert^{2}=\sum_{m\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\left\lVert\tilde{g}_{m}\right\rVert^{2}-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{k}|}\left\lVert\sum_{m\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\tilde{g}_{m}\right\rVert^{2}.

The first term ∑m=1M‖g~m‖2\sum_{m=1}^{M}\left\lVert\tilde{g}_{m}\right\rVert^{2} is independent of the clustering; therefore minimizing 𝒥k​-means\mathcal{J}_{k\text{-means}} is equivalent to maximizing

∑k=1K1|𝒞k|​‖∑m∈𝒞kg~m‖2.\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{k}|}\left\lVert\sum_{m\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\tilde{g}_{m}\right\rVert^{2}.

Under hard routing,

Gk=∑m∈𝒞kg~m,dk​(P)=|𝒞k|,G_{k}=\sum_{m\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\tilde{g}_{m},\qquad d_{k}(P)=|\mathcal{C}_{k}|,

hence

ℒ0,0(P;W)=−∑k=1K‖Gk‖2dk​(P)=−∑k=1K1|𝒞k|‖∑m∈𝒞kg~m‖2.\mathcal{L}_{0,0}(P;W)=-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\left\lVert G_{k}\right\rVert^{2}}{d_{k}(P)}=-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{k}|}\left\lVert\sum_{m\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\tilde{g}_{m}\right\rVert^{2}.

Thus minimizing ℒ0,0​(P,W)\mathcal{L}_{0,0}(P;W) is exactly equivalent to minimizing the k-means objective. ∎

Remark.

Experts correspond to clusters in gradient space, and routing corresponds to assignments. Soft routing probabilities pm​k∈[0,1]p_{mk}\in[0,1] therefore induce a relaxed k-means formulation.

B.3 Spectral Relaxation

Theorem B.2 (Spectral relaxation of load-normalized alignment).

Under nonempty hard routing,

ℒ0,0(P;W)=−∑k=1K1|𝒞k|‖∑m∈𝒞kg~m‖2.\mathcal{L}_{0,0}(P;W)=-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{k}|}\left\|\sum_{m\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\tilde{g}_{m}\right\|^{2}.

Define the gradient affinity matrix W∈ℝM×M,Wi​j:=⟨g~i,g~j⟩.W\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M},W_{ij}:=\left\langle\tilde{g}_{i},\tilde{g}_{j}\right\rangle. Then minimizing ℒ0,0​(P,W)\mathcal{L}_{0,0}(P;W) is equivalent to maximizing the ratio association objective

max⁡∑k=1K{𝒞k}k=1K⁡1|𝒞k|​∑i,j∈𝒞kWi​j.\max_{\{\mathcal{C}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{k}|}\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}W_{ij}.

Moreover, its standard continuous relaxation yields a top-KK eigenvector solution.

Proof.

First expand each cluster term:

‖∑m∈𝒞kg~m‖2=∑i∈𝒞k∑j∈𝒞k⟨g~i,g~j⟩=∑i,j∈𝒞kWi​j.\left\|\sum_{m\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\tilde{g}_{m}\right\|^{2}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\left\langle\tilde{g}_{i},\tilde{g}_{j}\right\rangle=\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}W_{ij}.

Hence

−ℒ0,0​(P,W)=∑k=1K1|𝒞k|​∑i,j∈𝒞kWi​j,-\mathcal{L}_{0,0}(P;W)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{k}|}\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}W_{ij},

which is exactly the ratio association objective.

To express it in trace form, let H∈{0,1}M×KH\in\{0,1\}^{M\times K} be the hard assignment matrix, where Hi​k=1H_{ik}=1 iff i∈𝒞ki\in\mathcal{C}_{k}. Define

S:=H⊤​H=diag⁡(|𝒞1|,…,|𝒞K|).S:=H^{\top}H=\mathrm{diag}(|\mathcal{C}_{1}|,\dots,|\mathcal{C}_{K}|).

Let hkh_{k} denote the kk-th column of HH. Then

∑i,j∈𝒞kWi​j=hk⊤​W​hk,|𝒞k|=hk⊤​hk.\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}W_{ij}=h_{k}^{\top}Wh_{k},\qquad|\mathcal{C}_{k}|=h_{k}^{\top}h_{k}.

Therefore

−ℒ0,0​(P,W)=∑k=1Khk⊤​W​hkhk⊤​hk=Tr⁡(S−1​H⊤​W​H).-\mathcal{L}_{0,0}(P;W)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{h_{k}^{\top}Wh_{k}}{h_{k}^{\top}h_{k}}=\mathrm{Tr}\!\left(S^{-1}H^{\top}WH\right).

Define the normalized embedding

Y:=HS−1/2∈ℝM×K,Y⊤Y=IK.Y:=HS^{-1/2}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times K},\qquad Y^{\top}Y=I_{K}.

Then

−ℒ0,0​(P,W)=Tr⁡(Y⊤​W​Y),-\mathcal{L}_{0,0}(P;W)=\mathrm{Tr}\!\left(Y^{\top}WY\right),

where YY is constrained to arise from a discrete partition.

Relaxing the discreteness constraint and optimizing over all Y∈ℝM×KY\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times K} satisfying Y⊤​Y=IKY^{\top}Y=I_{K} gives

maxY⊤​Y=IK⁡Tr⁡(Y⊤​W​Y).\max_{Y^{\top}Y=I_{K}}\mathrm{Tr}(Y^{\top}WY).

By Ky Fan’s maximum principle, a maximizer is given by choosing the columns of YY as the top-KK eigenvectors of WW. ∎

Remark.

The load-normalized alignment term admits a spectral relaxation: it corresponds to ratio association graph partitioning on the gradient affinity graph WW. Hard routing recovers a discrete partition, while the standard orthogonal relaxation corresponds to a spectral embedding spanned by the top-KK eigenvectors of WW. The practical soft router is a separate differentiable relaxation of the hard partition.

Appendix C Routing Dynamics and Alignment Geometry

Guide to Appendix C.

This appendix analyzes load scaling, directional preference, and mode separation under a symmetric prototype model. An illustrative task-loss feedback model supplies a reference for the load comparison. Table 3 maps each property to its assumptions and formal result.

C.1 Idealized Theoretical Assumptions

We use a symmetric prototype model to isolate load feedback and the geometric preference for separating mixed gradient observations. The baseline result concerns its specified continuous-time feedback law; the alignment results concern fixed observation distributions and the stated assignment objectives.

Expert–manifold matching (K=CK=C).

We assume the number of experts equals the number of latent gradient manifolds:

K=C.K=C.

Each manifold c∈{1,…,C}c\in\{1,\dots,C\} is associated with a prototype unit direction uc∈ℝdu_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, ‖uc‖=1\|u_{c}\|=1. The ideal optimal configuration assigns one expert to each manifold.

Uniform manifold prior.

Training observations are drawn from the CC manifolds with equal probability:

Pr⁡(c)=1C.\Pr(c)=\frac{1}{C}.

Thus, no manifold has intrinsic frequency advantage. Any imbalance arises purely from routing dynamics.

Gradient concentration model.

Detached gradient observations follow g~|c=uc+ξ\tilde{g}\mid c=u_{c}+\xi, where

𝔼⁡[ξ∣c]=0,Cov⁡(ξ∣c)⪯σ2​I,𝔼⁡[g~∣c]=uc.\mathbb{E}[\xi\mid c]=0,\qquad\mathrm{Cov}(\xi\mid c)\preceq\sigma^{2}I,\qquad\mathbb{E}[\tilde{g}\mid c]=u_{c}.

We assume the diagonal second moment ν:=𝔼⁡[‖g~‖2∣c]\nu:=\mathbb{E}[\|\tilde{g}\|^{2}\mid c] is mode-independent, as in the symmetric noise model.

Pairwise-homogeneous prototype geometry.

Let Γa​b:=⟨ua,ub⟩\Gamma_{ab}:=\langle u_{a},u_{b}\rangle be the prototype Gram matrix. We use the equiangular specialization

Γa​b={1,a=b,ρ,a≠b,−1C−1≤ρ<1,\Gamma_{ab}=\begin{cases}1,&a=b,\\ \rho,&a\neq b,\end{cases}\qquad-\frac{1}{C-1}\leq\rho<1,

and assume that this Gram matrix is realizable in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} (rank⁡(Γ)≤d\operatorname{rank}(\Gamma)\leq d). The lower bound is the positive-semidefinite constraint for an equicorrelation Gram matrix, and ρ<1\rho<1 supplies the strict same-mode advantage. Prototype geometry and mode priors are separate assumptions of the model.

The coherence and directional-overlap quantities are then consequences of the same Gram matrix, rather than separate free parameters. Conditional independence and 𝔼⁡[g~∣c]=uc\mathbb{E}[\tilde{g}\mid c]=u_{c} give, for i≠ji\neq j,

𝔼[⟨g~i,g~j⟩∣ci=a,cj=b]=𝔼[⟨ua,g~⟩∣c=b]=Γa​b.\mathbb{E}[\langle\tilde{g}_{i},\tilde{g}_{j}\rangle\mid c_{i}=a,c_{j}=b]=\mathbb{E}[\langle u_{a},\tilde{g}\rangle\mid c=b]=\Gamma_{ab}.

Thus both quantities equal 11 for a=ba=b and ρ\rho for a≠ba\neq b. All scalar-coherence and purity reductions below inherit this specialization. For a general prototype Gram matrix, the pairwise term is instead wk⊤​Γ​wkw_{k}^{\top}\Gamma w_{k} and need not depend only on ∑cwk​c2\sum_{c}w_{kc}^{2}. The case ρ<0\rho<0, where gradients from different manifolds interfere destructively in expectation, is the strongest instance of the gap 1−ρ>01-\rho>0 and is not assumed separately.

Load and mixture within an expert.

For the finite-window calculations, fix an integer count Lk≥1L_{k}\geq 1 and draw LkL_{k} observations independently from a mixture with mode probabilities wk​cw_{kc}, where ∑cwk​c=1\sum_{c}w_{kc}=1. Here GkG_{k} is the unweighted sum of these observations; wk​cw_{kc} specifies their sampling distribution, rather than the realized empirical proportions in a particular window. These exact finite-window formulas use this fixed-count, independent sampling model:

𝔼​‖Gk‖2=Lk​ν+Lk​(Lk−1)​(∑cwk​c2+∑c≠c′wk​c​wk​c′​ρ).\mathbb{E}\|G_{k}\|^{2}=L_{k}\nu+L_{k}(L_{k}-1)\left(\sum_{c}w_{kc}^{2}+\sum_{c\neq c^{\prime}}w_{kc}w_{kc^{\prime}}\rho\right). (6)

Thus, to leading pairwise order in LkL_{k},

𝔼​‖Gk‖2=Lk2​(ρ+(1−ρ)​∑cwk​c2)+O⁡(Lk).\mathbb{E}\|G_{k}\|^{2}=L_{k}^{2}\left(\rho+(1-\rho)\sum_{c}w_{kc}^{2}\right)+O(L_{k}). (7)
Geometric implication of mixing.

Since ∑cwk​c2\sum_{c}w_{kc}^{2} is maximized (equal to 11) when expert kk receives a single manifold, and minimized (equal to 1/C1/C) under uniform mixing, Equation (6) shows, at fixed Lk>1L_{k}>1:

  • •

    A single-manifold sampling distribution maximizes 𝔼​‖Gk‖2\mathbb{E}\|G_{k}\|^{2}.

  • •

    Mixing reduces expected coherence in proportion to the pairwise gap 1−ρ1-\rho.

  • •

    A smaller cross-manifold overlap ρ\rho increases this mixing penalty.

Initial symmetry.

We assume symmetric initialization:

pk​(0)=1K,κk​(0)=κ0.p_{k}(0)=\frac{1}{K},\qquad\kappa_{k}(0)=\kappa_{0}.

Thus, no expert has intrinsic advantage. Any asymmetry emerges dynamically.

Continuous-time routing abstraction.

We analyze routing via a continuous-time approximation of soft probability updates, treating

p⁡(t)∈ΔK−1.p(t)\in\Delta^{K-1}.

This allows direct stability and limit analysis.

C.2 Baseline Reference: An Illustrative Load-Feedback Model

Under the idealized assumptions in §C.1, we first analyze the baseline case where routing is driven solely by task loss (no alignment regularizer). We show that even under a symmetric initialization, an arbitrarily small early advantage can be amplified into a winner-take-all collapse (a simplex vertex attractor) via a positive feedback loop between load allocation and learning speed under the following competence–loss and load-driven learning dynamics.

(1) Uniform start with a small perturbation.

We consider a soft routing state p⁡(t)∈ΔK−1p(t)\in\Delta^{K-1} with symmetric initialization pk​(0)=1/Kp_{k}(0)=1/K. A “small perturbation” means that for some pair of experts i≠ji\neq j,

pi​(0)=1K+η,pj​(0)=1K−η,0<η≪1,p_{i}(0)=\frac{1}{K}+\eta,\qquad p_{j}(0)=\frac{1}{K}-\eta,\qquad 0<\eta\ll 1,

and optionally a matching competence perturbation κi​(0)>κj​(0)\kappa_{i}(0)>\kappa_{j}(0). Such asymmetry can arise from stochastic optimization noise or finite-sample effects.

Competence–loss coupling and load-driven learning.

We assume

ℓk​(t)=ℓ0−a​κk​(t),a>0,\ell_{k}(t)=\ell_{0}-a\,\kappa_{k}(t),\qquad a>0, (8)

and load-driven competence dynamics

κ˙k​(t)=α​pk​(t),α>0.\dot{\kappa}_{k}(t)=\alpha\,p_{k}(t),\qquad\alpha>0. (9)
(2) Ratio dynamics ⇒\Rightarrow positive feedback.

We model the baseline router update by replicator dynamics with payoff Πk​(t)=−ℓk​(t)\Pi_{k}(t)=-\ell_{k}(t):

p˙k​(t)=β​pk​(t)​(ℓ¯​(t)−ℓk​(t)),β>0,\dot{p}_{k}(t)=\beta\,p_{k}(t)\big(\bar{\ell}(t)-\ell_{k}(t)\big),\qquad\beta>0, (10)

where ℓ¯​(t)=∑j=1Kpj​(t)​ℓj​(t)\bar{\ell}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{K}p_{j}(t)\ell_{j}(t). For any two experts i,ji,j, define ri​j​(t)=pi​(t)/pj​(t)r_{ij}(t)=p_{i}(t)/p_{j}(t). A standard identity of replicator dynamics gives

dd​t​log⁡ri​j​(t)=β⁡(ℓj​(t)−ℓi​(t)).\frac{d}{dt}\log r_{ij}(t)=\beta\big(\ell_{j}(t)-\ell_{i}(t)\big). (11)

Substituting (8) yields

dd​t​log⁡ri​j​(t)=β​a​(κi​(t)−κj​(t)).\frac{d}{dt}\log r_{ij}(t)=\beta a\big(\kappa_{i}(t)-\kappa_{j}(t)\big). (12)

Meanwhile, from (9),

dd​t​(κi​(t)−κj​(t))=α⁡(pi​(t)−pj​(t)).\frac{d}{dt}\big(\kappa_{i}(t)-\kappa_{j}(t)\big)=\alpha\big(p_{i}(t)-p_{j}(t)\big). (13)

Equations (12)–(13) form a closed positive feedback loop: a small competence advantage increases routing probability, which further increases competence.

(3) Strict collapse in the two-expert case (K=2K=2).

The analytically tractable case is K=2K=2. Let p2​(t)=1−p1​(t)p_{2}(t)=1-p_{1}(t) and define the competence gap Δ​κ​(t)=κ1​(t)−κ2​(t)\Delta\kappa(t)=\kappa_{1}(t)-\kappa_{2}(t). From (13),

Δ​κ˙​(t)=α⁡(2​p1​(t)−1),\dot{\Delta\kappa}(t)=\alpha(2p_{1}(t)-1), (14)

and from (12) with r⁡(t)=p1​(t)/(1−p1​(t))r(t)=p_{1}(t)/(1-p_{1}(t)),

dd​t​log⁡p1​(t)1−p1​(t)=β​a​Δ​κ​(t).\frac{d}{dt}\log\frac{p_{1}(t)}{1-p_{1}(t)}=\beta a\,\Delta\kappa(t). (15)
Proposition C.1 (Winner-take-all under a small initial advantage).

Assume K=2K=2, an initial routing advantage, and no initial competence deficit:

p1​(0)>12andΔ​κ​(0)≥0.p_{1}(0)>\tfrac{1}{2}\quad\text{and}\quad\Delta\kappa(0)\geq 0.

Then Δ​κ​(t)\Delta\kappa(t) is strictly increasing and

p1​(t)1−p1​(t)→∞⇒p1​(t)→1.\frac{p_{1}(t)}{1-p_{1}(t)}\to\infty\quad\Rightarrow\quad p_{1}(t)\to 1.
Proof.

Let T=sup{t≥0:p1​(u)>12​ for all ​u∈[0,t)}T=\sup\{t\geq 0:p_{1}(u)>\tfrac{1}{2}\text{ for all }u\in[0,t)\}, which is positive by continuity. On [0,T)[0,T), (14) gives Δ​κ˙>0\dot{\Delta\kappa}>0, so Δ​κ​(t)≥Δ​κ​(0)≥0\Delta\kappa(t)\geq\Delta\kappa(0)\geq 0, and (15) then gives dd​t​log⁡p11−p1≥0\frac{d}{dt}\log\frac{p_{1}}{1-p_{1}}\geq 0, so p1​(t)≥p1​(0)>12p_{1}(t)\geq p_{1}(0)>\tfrac{1}{2}. If TT were finite, continuity would give p1​(T)=12p_{1}(T)=\tfrac{1}{2}, a contradiction; hence p1​(t)≥p1​(0)p_{1}(t)\geq p_{1}(0) for all t≥0t\geq 0. Consequently Δ​κ˙​(t)≥c:=α⁡(2​p1​(0)−1)>0\dot{\Delta\kappa}(t)\geq c:=\alpha(2p_{1}(0)-1)>0, so Δ​κ\Delta\kappa is strictly increasing with Δ​κ​(t)≥Δ​κ​(0)+c​t\Delta\kappa(t)\geq\Delta\kappa(0)+ct, and

log⁡p1​(t)1−p1​(t)≥log⁡p1​(0)1−p1​(0)+β​a​(Δ​κ​(0)​t+c2​t2)⟶∞,\log\frac{p_{1}(t)}{1-p_{1}(t)}\geq\log\frac{p_{1}(0)}{1-p_{1}(0)}+\beta a\Big(\Delta\kappa(0)\,t+\tfrac{c}{2}t^{2}\Big)\longrightarrow\infty,

so p1​(t)→1p_{1}(t)\to 1. ∎

Extension to K>2K>2 (pairwise domination).

For general KK, assume pk​(0)>0p_{k}(0)>0 for every expert. The ratio identity (11) then holds for every pair (i,j)(i,j). A competence advantage κk⋆​(t)>κj​(t)\kappa_{k^{\star}}(t)>\kappa_{j}(t) over a finite interval increases log⁡(pk⋆/pj)\log(p_{k^{\star}}/p_{j}) during that interval. The asymptotic behavior follows from the integrated competence advantage: integrating (12) gives

log⁡pk⋆​(t)pj​(t)=log⁡pk⋆​(0)pj​(0)+β​a​∫0t(κk⋆​(u)−κj​(u))​𝑑u.\log\frac{p_{k^{\star}}(t)}{p_{j}(t)}=\log\frac{p_{k^{\star}}(0)}{p_{j}(0)}+\beta a\int_{0}^{t}\big(\kappa_{k^{\star}}(u)-\kappa_{j}(u)\big)\,du. (16)

Consequently, a sufficient condition for pk⋆​(t)→1p_{k^{\star}}(t)\to 1 is

∫0t(κk⋆​(u)−κj​(u))​𝑑u⟶+∞for every ​j≠k⋆.\int_{0}^{t}\big(\kappa_{k^{\star}}(u)-\kappa_{j}(u)\big)\,du\longrightarrow+\infty\qquad\text{for every }j\neq k^{\star}.

Under this condition, all ratios pj​(t)/pk⋆​(t)p_{j}(t)/p_{k^{\star}}(t) tend to zero, and pk⋆​(t)=[1+∑j≠k⋆pj​(t)/pk⋆​(t)]−1→1p_{k^{\star}}(t)=[1+\sum_{j\neq k^{\star}}p_{j}(t)/p_{k^{\star}}(t)]^{-1}\to 1. This integrated-advantage condition extends the two-expert result to arbitrary KK.

C.3 GAR – Case 1: Load-Normalized Anti-Amplification under Homogeneous Mixing

We first analyze the load dependence of the alignment objective under the independent finite-window model. Assume that each expert receives a statistically homogeneous mixture of manifolds, i.e.,

wk​c=1Cfor all ​k,c,w_{kc}=\frac{1}{C}\quad\text{for all }k,c,

so that all experts have identical internal conflict statistics, but their total loads LkL_{k} may differ.

Expected coherence under homogeneous mixing.

Substituting wk​c=1/Cw_{kc}=1/C into (6) gives the exact identity

𝔼​‖Gk‖2=γ​Lk2+(ν−γ)​Lk,γ:=ρ+(1−ρ)/C.\mathbb{E}\|G_{k}\|^{2}=\gamma L_{k}^{2}+(\nu-\gamma)L_{k},\qquad\gamma:=\rho+(1-\rho)/C. (17)

For independent draws, γ=‖𝔼​g~‖2≥0\gamma=\|\mathbb{E}\tilde{g}\|^{2}\geq 0 and ν−γ=𝔼​‖g~−𝔼​g~‖2≥0\nu-\gamma=\mathbb{E}\|\tilde{g}-\mathbb{E}\tilde{g}\|^{2}\geq 0.

Alignment utility scaling.

Define the per-expert utility Uk​(P):=‖Gk​(P)‖2/(dk​(P)+ϵ)U_{k}(P):=\|G_{k}(P)\|^{2}/(d_{k}(P)+\epsilon), the kk-th term of 𝒜ϵ​(P,W)\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}(P;W) under the gradient-Gram affinity. At a hard assignment dk​(P)=Lkd_{k}(P)=L_{k}, so

Uk=‖Gk‖2Lk+ϵ.U_{k}=\frac{\|G_{k}\|^{2}}{L_{k}+\epsilon}.

Taking expectation while keeping the stabilizer explicit gives

𝔼⁡[Uk]=γ​Lk2+(ν−γ)​LkLk+ϵ=γ​Lk+(ν−γ−γ​ϵ)​LkLk+ϵ.\mathbb{E}[U_{k}]=\frac{\gamma L_{k}^{2}+(\nu-\gamma)L_{k}}{L_{k}+\epsilon}=\gamma L_{k}+\frac{(\nu-\gamma-\gamma\epsilon)L_{k}}{L_{k}+\epsilon}. (18)

Thus, for fixed ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0, load normalization converts the quadratic leading term into 𝔼⁡[Uk]=γ​Lk+O⁡(1)\mathbb{E}[U_{k}]=\gamma L_{k}+O(1). The exact per-unit utility is

𝔼⁡[Uk]Lk=γ​Lk+ν−γLk+ϵ⟶γ.\frac{\mathbb{E}[U_{k}]}{L_{k}}=\frac{\gamma L_{k}+\nu-\gamma}{L_{k}+\epsilon}\longrightarrow\gamma.

It exceeds γ\gamma by (ν−γ−γ​ϵ)/(Lk+ϵ)(\nu-\gamma-\gamma\epsilon)/(L_{k}+\epsilon), a gap that vanishes as the load grows.

Marginal alignment score.

Routing decisions depend on the row-wise derivative of Uk​(P)U_{k}(P) with respect to pm​kp_{mk}, evaluated where dk​(P)=Lkd_{k}(P)=L_{k}:

sm​k​(P)=∂Uk∂pm​k=2​⟨Gk,g~m⟩Lk+ϵ−‖Gk‖2(Lk+ϵ)2.s_{mk}(P)=\frac{\partial U_{k}}{\partial p_{mk}}=\frac{2\langle G_{k},\tilde{g}_{m}\rangle}{L_{k}+\epsilon}-\frac{\|G_{k}\|^{2}}{(L_{k}+\epsilon)^{2}}. (19)

Evaluate this derivative at a hard assignment containing observation mm, so that mm is one of the LkL_{k} independent samples already included in GkG_{k}. The self term must then be retained:

𝔼⁡⟨Gk,g~m⟩=ν+(Lk−1)​γ.\mathbb{E}\langle G_{k},\tilde{g}_{m}\rangle=\nu+(L_{k}-1)\gamma.

Combining this with (17) gives the exact expectation

𝔼⁡[sm​k​(P)]=γ⁡(1−ϵ2(Lk+ϵ)2)+(ν−γ)​Lk+2​ϵ(Lk+ϵ)2.\mathbb{E}[s_{mk}(P)]=\gamma\left(1-\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{(L_{k}+\epsilon)^{2}}\right)+(\nu-\gamma)\frac{L_{k}+2\epsilon}{(L_{k}+\epsilon)^{2}}. (20)

In particular, at ϵ=0\epsilon=0, this equals γ+(ν−γ)/Lk\gamma+(\nu-\gamma)/L_{k}, which exceeds γ\gamma whenever the observations have nonzero variance. For fixed ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0, the expected score still converges to the finite limit γ\gamma as Lk→∞L_{k}\to\infty. The expectation is taken over an observation in the same finite sampling window.

Proposition C.2 (Load-normalized anti-amplification under homogeneous conflict).

Under the independent finite-window model with homogeneous mixing (wk​c=1/Cw_{kc}=1/C), integer Lk≥1L_{k}\geq 1, finite ν\nu, and fixed ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0, the load-normalized alignment channel removes the quadratic load amplification in 𝔼​‖Gk‖2\mathbb{E}\|G_{k}\|^{2}: 𝔼⁡[Uk]=γ​Lk+O⁡(1)\mathbb{E}[U_{k}]=\gamma L_{k}+O(1), and the expected in-window marginal score in (20) converges to γ\gamma. At ϵ=0\epsilon=0 it equals γ+(ν−γ)/Lk\gamma+(\nu-\gamma)/L_{k}, which is non-increasing in LkL_{k}, so additional load does not raise the expected marginal score.

Proof.

The utility identity follows by dividing (17) by Lk+ϵL_{k}+\epsilon. Substitution of the in-window self term into (19) yields (20). Taking Lk→∞L_{k}\to\infty with the mixture and ϵ\epsilon fixed gives the limits. At ϵ=0\epsilon=0, (20) reduces to γ+(ν−γ)/Lk\gamma+(\nu-\gamma)/L_{k}, which is non-increasing in LkL_{k} because ν≥γ\nu\geq\gamma. ∎

Remark.

In contrast to the baseline dynamics, where higher load can increase learning speed and further increase routing probability, the expected marginal score of the normalized alignment channel does not grow with load in this sampling model. The static coherence preference and the leading-order separation argument are treated separately in Appendix C.4–C.6.

C.4 GAR – Case 2: Static Directional Tilt and Coherence Preference

We compare fixed sampling mixtures at the same load. Enriching a mixture in one manifold tilts the mean surrogate aggregate toward that manifold and increases the expected coherence utility relative to uniform mixing.

Setup (mode prototype model).

Under §C.1, 𝔼⁡[g~∣c]=uc\mathbb{E}[\tilde{g}\mid c]=u_{c} and ‖uc‖=1\|u_{c}\|=1. Directional alignment and pairwise coherence are both governed by the single prototype-overlap gap 1−ρ>01-\rho>0. Let expert kk receive LkL_{k} independent observations from mixture probabilities wk​cw_{kc}, with integer Lk≥1L_{k}\geq 1 fixed. Each mode pair obeys the common coherence and prototype-overlap conditions in Section C.1.

Lemma C.3 (Directional tilt of the surrogate aggregate).

Under the fixed-mixture independent sampling model, the detached surrogate aggregate

Gk=∑m=1Lkg~mG_{k}=\sum_{m=1}^{L_{k}}\tilde{g}_{m}

satisfies

𝔼[Gk∣wk⋅]=Lk∑c=1Cwk​cuc.\mathbb{E}\!\left[G_{k}\mid w_{k\cdot}\right]=L_{k}\sum_{c=1}^{C}w_{kc}\,u_{c}. (21)
Proof.

Each observation has mean ∑cwk​c​uc\sum_{c}w_{kc}u_{c}. By linearity,

𝔼[Gk∣wk⋅]=∑m=1Lk∑c=1Cwk​cuc=Lk∑cwk​cuc.\mathbb{E}[G_{k}\mid w_{k\cdot}]=\sum_{m=1}^{L_{k}}\sum_{c=1}^{C}w_{kc}\,u_{c}=L_{k}\sum_{c}w_{kc}\,u_{c}.

∎

Remark.

Equation (21) shows that any small bias in wk​cw_{kc} immediately tilts the mean direction of GkG_{k} toward the corresponding prototype ucu_{c}.

Two technical lemmas used below are stated in Section C.5: Lemma C.6 formalizes the same-manifold alignment advantage, and Lemma C.7 shows that the per-load coherence utility strictly increases with mixture purity.

Remark.

For the symmetric perturbation below, independent samples from the enriched manifold become more aligned with the mean GkG_{k}, while those from each depleted manifold become less aligned. This comparison concerns the alignment component of the surrogate, with the mixtures held fixed.

Static comparison with uniform mixing.

Consider a manifold c⋆c^{\star} and an expert kk with a tiny initial enrichment

wk​c⋆=1C+δ,δ>0​arbitrarily small,w_{kc^{\star}}=\frac{1}{C}+\delta,\qquad\delta>0\ \text{arbitrarily small},

with the remaining mass spread across other manifolds. Then:

  • •

    By Lemma C.3, GkG_{k} tilts toward uc⋆u_{c^{\star}}.

  • •

    By Lemma C.6, mode-c⋆c^{\star} samples have larger expected alignment 𝔼​⟨Gk,g~⟩\mathbb{E}\langle G_{k},\tilde{g}\rangle than under uniform mixing.

  • •

    By Lemma C.7, the expert’s coherence utility UkU_{k} increases as its mixture becomes purer.

These comparisons quantify the objective preference for coherent observation clusters at fixed load.

Proposition C.4 (Static directional tilt and coherence preference).

Under the independent sampling model, assume C>1C>1, integer Lk>1L_{k}>1, ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0, and ρ<1\rho<1. Suppose expert kk is perturbed from a uniform mixture toward mode c⋆c^{\star} by

wk​c⋆=1C+δ,wk​c=1C−δC−1(c≠c⋆),w_{kc^{\star}}=\frac{1}{C}+\delta,\qquad w_{kc}=\frac{1}{C}-\frac{\delta}{C-1}\quad(c\neq c^{\star}),

where 0<δ<(C−1)/C0<\delta<(C-1)/C. Then the expected alignment of an independent mode-c⋆c^{\star} sample with GkG_{k} increases by

Lk​δ​(1−ρ)>0L_{k}\delta(1-\rho)>0

relative to uniform mixing. Moreover,

∑cwk​c2=1C+CC−1​δ2>1C,\sum_{c}w_{kc}^{2}=\frac{1}{C}+\frac{C}{C-1}\delta^{2}>\frac{1}{C},

so the expected coherence utility is larger than under uniform mixing by

Lk​(Lk−1)Lk+ϵ​(1−ρ)​CC−1​δ2>0.\frac{L_{k}(L_{k}-1)}{L_{k}+\epsilon}(1-\rho)\frac{C}{C-1}\delta^{2}>0.

The comparison holds for the stated fixed mixtures.

Proof.

For a mode-c⋆c^{\star} sample, Lemma C.6 gives

𝔼[⟨𝔼[Gk∣wk⋅],g~⟩∣c⋆]=Lk(wk​c⋆+(1−wk​c⋆)ρ).\mathbb{E}\!\big[\langle\mathbb{E}[G_{k}\mid w_{k\cdot}],\tilde{g}\rangle\mid c^{\star}\big]=L_{k}\left(w_{kc^{\star}}+(1-w_{kc^{\star}})\rho\right).

Relative to the uniform value obtained by setting wk​c⋆=1/Cw_{kc^{\star}}=1/C, the difference is

Lk​δ​(1−ρ)>0.L_{k}\delta(1-\rho)>0.

For the purity term,

∑cwk​c2=(1C+δ)2+(C−1)​(1C−δC−1)2=1C+CC−1​δ2.\sum_{c}w_{kc}^{2}=\left(\frac{1}{C}+\delta\right)^{2}+(C-1)\left(\frac{1}{C}-\frac{\delta}{C-1}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{C}+\frac{C}{C-1}\delta^{2}.

This is strictly larger than the uniform purity 1/C1/C for any δ>0\delta>0. Multiplying this purity increase by the slope in Lemma C.7 gives the stated utility difference. ∎

Remark C.5 (Relation between the alignment cases).

Case 2 characterizes directional alignment and coherence at fixed load. Case 3 varies the mode-to-expert assignment to analyze the corresponding leading-order separation preference.

C.5 Technical Lemmas for Static Directional Tilt

Lemma C.6 (Tilt implies same-manifold alignment advantage).

For an independent sample from manifold cc, the expected alignment with the mean surrogate aggregate satisfies

𝔼[⟨𝔼[Gk∣wk⋅],g~⟩|c]=Lk(wk​c+∑c′≠cwk​c′ρ).\mathbb{E}\!\left[\langle\mathbb{E}[G_{k}\mid w_{k\cdot}],\,\tilde{g}\rangle\,\middle|\,c\right]=L_{k}\left(w_{kc}+\sum_{c^{\prime}\neq c}w_{kc^{\prime}}\,\rho\right). (22)

Since ∑c′wk​c′=1\sum_{c^{\prime}}w_{kc^{\prime}}=1, the right-hand side can be written as Lk​[wk​c+(1−wk​c)​ρ]L_{k}[w_{kc}+(1-w_{kc})\rho], which is strictly increasing in wk​cw_{kc} whenever 1>ρ1>\rho.

Proof of Lemma C.6.

Using Lemma C.3, conditioning on cc and linearity,

𝔼⁡[⟨𝔼⁡[Gk∣wk],g~⟩∣c]=Lk​∑c′wk​c′​𝔼​[⟨uc′,g~⟩∣c].\mathbb{E}\!\left[\langle\mathbb{E}[G_{k}\mid w_{k}],\,\tilde{g}\rangle\mid c\right]=L_{k}\sum_{c^{\prime}}w_{kc^{\prime}}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\langle u_{c^{\prime}},\tilde{g}\rangle\mid c\right].

The prototype-overlap definitions give the two cases 11 for c′=cc^{\prime}=c and ρ\rho for c′≠cc^{\prime}\neq c, which yields (22). The coefficient of wk​cw_{kc} is 1−ρ>01-\rho>0. ∎

Lemma C.7 (Tilt increases per-load coherence utility for purer mixtures).

Under the independent sampling model, for fixed integer Lk>1L_{k}>1 and ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0, the finite-window expected utility

𝔼⁡[Uk]=Lk​ν+Lk​(Lk−1)​(ρ+(1−ρ)​∑cwk​c2)Lk+ϵ\mathbb{E}[U_{k}]=\frac{L_{k}\nu+L_{k}(L_{k}-1)\left(\rho+(1-\rho)\sum_{c}w_{kc}^{2}\right)}{L_{k}+\epsilon}

is strictly increasing in the purity measure ∑cwk​c2\sum_{c}w_{kc}^{2} whenever 1>ρ1>\rho.

Proof of Lemma C.7.

The expression follows from (6). For fixed LkL_{k}, it is affine in ∑cwk​c2\sum_{c}w_{kc}^{2} with slope

Lk​(Lk−1)​(1−ρ)Lk+ϵ>0.\frac{L_{k}(L_{k}-1)(1-\rho)}{L_{k}+\epsilon}>0.

Thus purer mixtures have larger expected per-load coherence utility. ∎

C.6 GAR – Case 3: Collapsed Assignments Are Not Local Maxima

We now show that, under the geometric mode assumptions in §C.1, a collapsed assignment is not a local maximum of the leading-order alignment surrogate over continuous mode-to-expert assignments. An arbitrarily small mode-separating perturbation strictly increases this surrogate.

Here the leading-order objective is defined at ϵ=0\epsilon=0 after dropping finite-window corrections; its boundary is analyzed directly in that limit. The theorem characterizes a static separation preference of this limiting objective rather than the trajectory of a trained router.

Alignment surrogate as a purity functional.

Recall Uk=‖Gk‖2/(Lk+ϵ)U_{k}=\|G_{k}\|^{2}/(L_{k}+\epsilon). Setting ϵ=0\epsilon=0 and retaining only the leading O⁡(Lk)O(L_{k}) term after dividing (7) by LkL_{k} gives the purity-dependent utility

𝔼⁡[Uk]≈Lk​(ρ+(1−ρ)​∑c=1Cwk​c2).\mathbb{E}[U_{k}]\;\approx\;L_{k}\Big(\rho+(1-\rho)\sum_{c=1}^{C}w_{kc}^{2}\Big). (23)

Thus the expected alignment reward has purity-dependent part

ℛ⁡(p)=ρ​∑kLk+(1−ρ)​∑kLk​∑cwk​c2.\mathcal{R}(p)=\rho\sum_{k}L_{k}+(1-\rho)\sum_{k}L_{k}\sum_{c}w_{kc}^{2}. (24)

Since ∑kLk\sum_{k}L_{k} is fixed, maximizing ℛ\mathcal{R} is equivalent to maximizing

Φ:=∑k=1KLk​∑c=1Cwk​c2.\Phi:=\sum_{k=1}^{K}L_{k}\sum_{c=1}^{C}w_{kc}^{2}. (25)

Because 1>ρ1>\rho, increasing Φ\Phi strictly increases ℛ\mathcal{R}. Here loads are continuous mode masses. If xk​c≥0x_{kc}\geq 0 is the mass of mode cc assigned to expert kk, then Lk=∑cxk​cL_{k}=\sum_{c}x_{kc} and Lk​∑cwk​c2=∑cxk​c2/LkL_{k}\sum_{c}w_{kc}^{2}=\sum_{c}x_{kc}^{2}/L_{k} for Lk>0L_{k}>0. We define the contribution of an empty expert to be zero, its continuous extension at Lk=0L_{k}=0. Locality is measured in these mode masses.

Collapsed vertex implies maximal mixing.

Consider the (collapsed) vertex state in which a single expert k⋆k^{\star} receives all load:

Lk⋆=L,Lj=0(j≠k⋆).L_{k^{\star}}=L,\qquad L_{j}=0\ \ (j\neq k^{\star}).

Under the uniform manifold prior Pr⁡(c)=1/C\Pr(c)=1/C, this implies the dominant expert receives the entire mixture, i.e.,

wk⋆​c=1C∀c.w_{k^{\star}c}=\frac{1}{C}\quad\forall c.

Then the weighted purity equals

Φcoll=L​∑c=1C(1C)2=LC.\Phi_{\mathrm{coll}}=L\sum_{c=1}^{C}\left(\frac{1}{C}\right)^{2}=\frac{L}{C}. (26)
A separating perturbation strictly increases purity.

We now show that the collapsed state is not locally optimal for Φ\Phi by constructing an arbitrarily small perturbation that increases it.

Fix any manifold c0c_{0}. Move an infinitesimal amount of load δ>0\delta>0 consisting solely of mode-c0c_{0} observations from expert k⋆k^{\star} to an unused expert jj. Then

Lj=δ,Lk⋆=L−δ.L_{j}=\delta,\qquad L_{k^{\star}}=L-\delta.

Expert jj becomes pure for c0c_{0}, hence

wj​c0=1,wj​c=0(c≠c0),⇒∑cwj​c2=1.w_{jc_{0}}=1,\qquad w_{jc}=0\ (c\neq c_{0}),\quad\Rightarrow\quad\sum_{c}w_{jc}^{2}=1.

For the remaining dominant expert k⋆k^{\star}, the mode counts are L/C−δL/C-\delta for c0c_{0} and L/CL/C for every other mode, so

∑cwk⋆​c2=(L/C−δ)2+(C−1)​(L/C)2(L−δ)2=1C+(1−1C)​δ2(L−δ)2.\sum_{c}w_{k^{\star}c}^{2}=\frac{(L/C-\delta)^{2}+(C-1)(L/C)^{2}}{(L-\delta)^{2}}=\frac{1}{C}+\left(1-\frac{1}{C}\right)\frac{\delta^{2}}{(L-\delta)^{2}}. (27)

Therefore, the perturbed weighted purity satisfies

Φpert\displaystyle\Phi_{\mathrm{pert}} =(L−δ)​∑cwk⋆​c2+δ\displaystyle=(L-\delta)\sum_{c}w_{k^{\star}c}^{2}+\delta
=LC+δ⁡(1−1C)+(1−1C)​δ2L−δ.\displaystyle=\frac{L}{C}+\delta\left(1-\frac{1}{C}\right)+\left(1-\frac{1}{C}\right)\frac{\delta^{2}}{L-\delta}. (28)

For any C>1C>1 and sufficiently small 0<δ<L/C0<\delta<L/C, every added term is positive:

Φpert−Φcoll>0.\Phi_{\mathrm{pert}}-\Phi_{\mathrm{coll}}>0.

Hence Φ\Phi (and thus ℛ\mathcal{R}) can be strictly increased by an arbitrarily small separating perturbation.

Theorem C.8 (Collapsed assignments are not local maxima of the alignment surrogate).

Consider the continuous mode-mass surrogate (24), with total mass L>0L>0, uniform mode masses L/CL/C, K=C>1K=C>1, and 1>ρ1>\rho. An assignment sending all mass to a single expert is not a local maximum of ℛ\mathcal{R}: every neighborhood contains a feasible mode-separating assignment with strictly larger reward.

Proof.

The perturbation above preserves every mode’s total mass and is feasible for 0<δ<L/C0<\delta<L/C. Its distance from the collapsed assignment tends to zero as δ→0\delta\to 0. Equations (24) and (28) give

ℛpert−ℛcoll=(1−ρ)​(1−1C)​(δ+δ2L−δ)>0.\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{pert}}-\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{coll}}=(1-\rho)\left(1-\frac{1}{C}\right)\left(\delta+\frac{\delta^{2}}{L-\delta}\right)>0.

Thus every neighborhood contains a strictly improving feasible assignment, which excludes a local maximum. ∎

Synthesis.

In the illustrative baseline model, collapse arises from a load–learning positive feedback: more load ⇒\Rightarrow faster learning ⇒\Rightarrow lower loss ⇒\Rightarrow more load. The alignment channel introduces a competing geometric pressure: mixed experts reduce the weighted purity Φ\Phi and thereby reduce the attainable alignment reward. The constructed separation of one mode from the collapsed mixture increases Φ\Phi and hence ℛ\mathcal{R}. Multiplying the reward by λ>0\lambda>0 preserves this static preference.

Together, the three cases establish that the expected marginal score does not grow with load, directional preference for coherent mixtures, and an improving separation direction at collapsed assignments under their respective assumptions. The implemented router combines the task-loss gradient with the weighted alignment gradient, as specified in Algorithm 1.

Appendix D Hyperparameters and Reproducibility

D.1 Configuration Principles

The frozen LoRA-FFN top-4 comparisons, the trainable classification-head and full-FFN settings, the Qwen3-8B comparison, and the DeBERTa single-task controls use the selection protocol below within each setting. Both top-1 comparisons follow the same protocol (Appendices D.4 and D.6). Model-training learning rate and applicable method-specific coefficients are selected independently for each method. Baseline first selects its learning rate, gradient clipping, and weight decay by a coordinate-wise search followed by joint local confirmation within each setting and mixture. All other methods inherit its clipping and weight-decay selections, which are excluded from their own hyperparameter optimization (HPO). The warmup ratio is fixed at 0.10.1 for every method and setting. Baseline has three optimizer search coordinates but no method-specific coefficient. STGC+Load independently selects its model-training learning rate, βSTGC\beta_{\mathrm{STGC}}, and λload\lambda_{\mathrm{load}} within each setting and mixture under the shared HPO procedure. The 1,000-update RoBERTa LoRA-FFN and classification-head coefficient ablations cover the five E8K4 mixtures. Each setting and mixture reuses its selected GAR configuration; only λ\lambda varies within each sweep, with no additional HPO. The grouped configuration tables report the optimizer settings and method-specific coefficients used under these protocols. All supervised endpoint summaries average five seeds and describe variation conditional on the selected configurations.

The trainer uses a single AdamW parameter group for all trainable parameters, with (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.999)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.999) and optimizer ϵopt=10−8\epsilon_{\rm opt}=10^{-8}. Learning rate and weight decay follow the configuration tables; the warmup schedule is specified below. These AdamW moment and stability settings are fixed, not additional HPO coordinates.

For readability, continuous hyperparameters are displayed to at most two significant digits.

Final runs use the complete corresponding training split. Forward accuracy and routing-selection evaluation use the complete benchmark-provided labeled evaluation split; gradient diagnostics use the checkpoint probes defined in Appendix E. Evaluation splits, numerical precision, and runtime resources are detailed in Appendix D.11.

D.2 Frozen-Backbone LoRA-FFN Configurations

The frozen LoRA-FFN comparison covers seven methods on frozen RoBERTa, DeBERTa, and Qwen3-1.7B on five dataset mixtures containing five to eight tasks; their constituent datasets are listed in brackets in the result and configuration tables. All five mixtures use E8K4 routing and 2,000 optimizer updates, with a common batch schedule and evaluation protocol across methods within each backbone and mixture.

Shared batch schedule and candidate evaluation.

A DeBERTa CAGrad development-probe comparison selected the effective per-task batch and micro-batch sizes for each multi-task mixture. Those sizes are reused by the compared methods and backbones, including top-1 routing, classification-head, full-parameter FFN, and Qwen3-8B extensions. The transferred values are the batch sizes, not CAGrad’s learning rate or method coefficients. The shared candidate-evaluation procedure uses a fixed 10% training-derived probe, training on the remaining 90%, and scores final-checkpoint equal-task macro accuracy. All methods in every comparison use this candidate-evaluation protocol.

A multi-task update consumes one batch from each task loader. Fixed update budgets are used because the mixed-task schedule has no single epoch count. For a mixture of TT tasks in Table 4, each update uses 32​T32T examples: a batch of 32 per task, split into four same-task groups of eight. These schedules apply to all compared methods and backbones.

Optimizer and coefficient selection.

For each backbone, adaptation setting, and mixture, Baseline is searched first over learning rate, gradient clipping in [0.5,2.0][0.5,2.0], and weight decay in [0,0.05][0,0.05]. These three coordinates are included in Baseline’s coordinate-wise selection and local confirmation under the candidate budget below. Its selected clipping and weight decay are then locked for all other methods in that comparison. Different mixtures or settings may use different selected values. The warmup ratio is fixed globally at 0.10.1 and is excluded from HPO. Learning rate increases linearly over the first 10% of optimizer updates and remains constant at the method’s selected rate thereafter.

Each non-Baseline method tunes its own model-training learning rate and applicable coefficients: CAGrad’s cc, GAR’s λalign\lambda_{\mathrm{align}}, the respective STGC, LoadPen, and SwitchAux coefficients, and both βSTGC\beta_{\mathrm{STGC}} and λload\lambda_{\mathrm{load}} for STGC+Load. CAGrad’s inner learning rate controls its gradient-combination solver and is distinct from the model-training learning rate; it is fixed at 0.10.1 in every setting, including both top-1 extensions and the single-task controls, and is not searched. Gradient clipping and weight decay remain fixed during these subsequent searches and all final runs within each setting and mixture; warmup is always fixed. The STGC conflict threshold is fixed at τSTGC=0\tau_{\mathrm{STGC}}=0. Baseline has no method-specific coefficient to tune.

The model-training learning-rate reference range is [2×10−6,5×10−3][2\times 10^{-6},5\times 10^{-3}] on a log scale. The coefficient reference ranges are CAGrad c∈[0.1,1.0]c\in[0.1,1.0], λalign∈[10−5,3×10−2]\lambda_{\mathrm{align}}\in[10^{-5},3\times 10^{-2}], STGC [0.25,4][0.25,4], LoadPen [10−6,1.1×10−2][10^{-6},1.1\times 10^{-2}], and SwitchAux [10−6,1.3×10−2][10^{-6},1.3\times 10^{-2}]. STGC+Load uses the STGC range for βSTGC\beta_{\mathrm{STGC}} and the LoadPen range for λload\lambda_{\mathrm{load}}. Selection uses the training-derived probe described above.

HPO uses one coordinate-wise pass with eight candidate values per free coordinate, followed by local confirmation. Initial candidates are equally spaced on a log scale for the learning rate, λalign\lambda_{\mathrm{align}}, βSTGC\beta_{\mathrm{STGC}}, λload\lambda_{\mathrm{load}}, and the SwitchAux coefficient, and on a linear scale for clipping, weight decay, and CAGrad cc. Each candidate is evaluated with two shared random seeds, using 500 optimizer updates for multi-task selection or one complete training-loader epoch for single-task selection. Final evaluations use five shared random seeds and the final-run budgets listed for each setting; the selection and final-run budgets are distinct. For dd active coordinates (d≤3d\leq 3 for every method), local confirmation uses a three-point Cartesian grid on all dd coordinates, giving 3d3^{d} nominal evaluations. Each local coordinate uses the current best value and two reproducibly sampled nearby values within its reference range. Thus final selections need not lie on the initial grid. Baseline has d=3d=3 (learning rate, clipping, and weight decay), giving 8×3=248\times 3=24 coordinate-sweep and 33=273^{3}=27 local-confirmation candidates (51 in total). CAGrad, GAR, STGC, LoadPen, and SwitchAux each have d=2d=2 (learning rate and one method coefficient), giving 8×2=168\times 2=16 coordinate-sweep and 32=93^{2}=9 local-confirmation candidates (25 in total). STGC+Load has d=3d=3 (learning rate, βSTGC\beta_{\mathrm{STGC}}, and λload\lambda_{\mathrm{load}}), giving 8×3=248\times 3=24 coordinate-sweep and 3×3×3=273\times 3\times 3=27 local-confirmation candidates (51 in total). Fixed clip/WD settings are not reintroduced as search axes. All methods use the same per-coordinate search density and per-candidate evaluation protocol; total candidate counts follow the number of free coordinates. Each method selects its own learning rate and applicable coefficients under this shared selection procedure.

The frozen LoRA-FFN experiments use LoRA rank 1616, LoRA scaling α=16\alpha=16, and dropout 0.10.1. At the final transformer layer’s feed-forward block, the base intermediate and output modules are retained, and routed LoRA experts add hidden-to-rank-to-hidden residual deltas, following the low-rank parameterization of LoRA (Hu et al., 2022). The routing objectives use ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8} for numerical stabilization. These fixed architectural choices are held constant across methods within a setting.

All five mixtures use E8K4 and sequence length 256. RoBERTa and DeBERTa use FP32, and Qwen3-1.7B uses BF16.

Task-specific prediction heads.

The frozen top-4 LoRA-FFN models share the backbone and routed FFN modules and use a separate linear prediction head for each task. Label indices are local to a task: the same index can denote entailment, acceptability, or a sentiment category in different datasets. Separate heads avoid forcing these distinct label meanings onto the same output weights, while retaining the shared representation in which task gradients can interact. Each head has the output width of its task; ANLI and CB therefore use three logits, and binary tasks use two, with no padding logits. Task identity selects the prediction head and corresponding loss; it is not supplied as an explicit router input. The router receives token hidden states, so any task structure in its assignments must be learned from those representations and the training signals. All compared methods within this setting use the same head design.

The configuration tables are grouped by backbone and task count to match the corresponding result tables. Each row gives the final optimizer settings and method coefficients for that comparison.

D.2.1 RoBERTa

Tables 5 and 6 report the selected learning rates, fixed clipping and weight-decay settings, and applicable method-specific coefficients for each mixture.

D.2.2 DeBERTa

We use DeBERTaV3-base (He et al., 2023). Tables 7 and 8 report the selected learning rates, fixed clipping and weight-decay settings, and applicable method-specific coefficients for each mixture.

D.2.3 Qwen3-1.7B

Following the Baseline-first selection procedure above, the selected clipping values are shared within each mixture; the selected weight decay is 0.010.01 throughout. Subsequent method searches tune model learning rate and applicable coefficients while inheriting these controls. Warmup remains fixed at 0.10.1. Tables 9 and 10 report the final configurations.

D.3 Qwen3-8B Final Configurations

The three Qwen3-8B methods reuse the shared per-mixture batch and micro-batch sizes and the Baseline-first HPO procedure described in Appendix D.2. Final evaluation uses five seeds with 2,000 updates and BF16. The selected weight decay is 0.010 throughout and is shared across methods within each mixture; CAGrad’s inner learning rate is fixed at 0.10. GAR uses load normalization. Token routing and auxiliary group averaging follow Section 5. The LoRA experts, per-task prediction heads, sequence length, and warmup follow Appendix D.2. Table 11 reports the selected values to two significant digits. All five mixtures use eight experts with top-4 routing and 32 examples per task with micro-batches of eight.

D.4 Frozen RoBERTa Top-1 LoRA-FFN

This extension evaluates Baseline, CAGrad, and GAR on the same five dataset mixtures with frozen RoBERTa-base and eight rank-16 LoRA experts (α=16\alpha=16) in the final-layer FFN. One expert is selected per token (E8K1). Training uses FP32, sequence length 256, the per-task batch size 32 and micro-batch size 8 of Appendix D.2, warmup ratio 0.10.1, and 2,000 optimizer updates. Final evaluations use the full labeled evaluation splits and the same five shared random seeds.

Straight-through top-1 routing.

For token-router logits zz, define σ=softmax⁡(z)\sigma=\operatorname{softmax}(z) at unit temperature and o=onehot⁡(arg⁡maxe⁡ze)o=\operatorname{onehot}(\arg\max_{e}z_{e}). The configured gate is

π⁡(z)=stopgrad⁡(o−σ)+σ.\pi(z)=\mathrm{stopgrad}(o-\sigma)+\sigma.

Its forward value is exactly one-hot, while its backward derivative is the full-softmax Jacobian. All three methods use this rule in the task forward computation. GAR also uses it when recomputing auxiliary gates from detached routing inputs. The auxiliary branch averages the configured gates over each example’s valid tokens and then over the examples in each same-task micro-batch. It pairs these group probabilities with detached expert-gradient observations and uses the load-normalized objective of Section 5, with ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}.

Prediction heads and configurations.

Each task has its own linear prediction head, as in the frozen top-4 setting, with three outputs for ANLI and CB and two for the binary tasks. Gradient clipping and weight decay are shared within each mixture; Table 12 gives the selected method-specific learning rates and coefficients. CAGrad’s inner learning rate is fixed at 0.10.1; the selected λalign\lambda_{\mathrm{align}} values are 1.2​e−31.2\mathrm{e}{-3}, 1​e−31\mathrm{e}{-3}, 1​e−31\mathrm{e}{-3}, 1.2​e−31.2\mathrm{e}{-3}, and 1​e−31\mathrm{e}{-3} for the five-task, six-task, seven-task (PAWS), seven-task (MRPC), and eight-task mixtures, respectively. GAR uses load normalization.

Search protocol.

The top-1 search uses the candidate-evaluation protocol of Appendix D.2: 500 updates with two shared random seeds, training on 90% of each training split and scoring final-checkpoint macro accuracy on its fixed 10% development probe. Baseline first searches its model-training learning rate, clipping, and weight decay over the reference ranges in Appendix D.2. After local confirmation, CAGrad and GAR inherit only Baseline’s selected clipping and weight decay. CAGrad searches its own model-training learning rate and cc, fixing its inner learning rate at 0.10.1; GAR searches its own learning rate and λalign\lambda_{\mathrm{align}}. Each free coordinate receives eight candidates, followed by a three-point local grid on all dd free coordinates. Baseline therefore uses 51 candidate configurations, and CAGrad and GAR each use 25. The batch schedule remains fixed throughout selection and the 2,000-update final runs.

D.5 Trainable RoBERTa Classification-Head MoE

The compared methods use the same batch schedule, update budget, and evaluation protocol within this extension. Baseline first selects learning rate, clipping, and weight decay using Appendix D.2’s procedure. Subsequent methods inherit the selected clipping and weight decay and tune their own learning rates and applicable coefficients. Warmup is fixed at 0.10.1.

This setting uses the same routing objective and implementation pathway to test whether the five-to-eight-task accuracy gain and the routing trade-off depend on expert placement and trainability, and to record full routing-diagnostic trajectories. It differs from the frozen LoRA-FFN setting on three axes at once. First, the RoBERTa-base backbone is fully trainable. Second, the experts are rank-16 LoRA deltas (scaling α=16\alpha=16, dropout 0.10.1) applied to the classification head over a shared base head, so the combined logits are base⁡(h)+∑kpk​Δk​(h)\mathrm{base}(h)+\sum_{k}p_{k}\,\Delta_{k}(h) for the pooled representation hh. Every task in a mixture uses this same logit space. The output width is three when the mixture contains a three-way task (ANLI or CB), and two otherwise. Binary-task targets remain indexed by {0,1}\{0,1\} in a three-logit mixture; the third logit participates in the common softmax normalization but is never a binary-task target. The shared-width rule is identical for every compared method in the classification-head setting. Third, the router is a linear map on the masked-mean pooled representation, so routing is sequence-level, using top-4 masked-softmax routing over eight experts (E8K4) in all five mixtures. Router numerics are FP32; the remaining forward and backward computation uses BF16.

Shared-output stress test.

We use this extension to examine routing under a shared prediction space. It has no task-specific output head: the shared base head and the input-conditioned mixture of expert deltas jointly produce the logits. Task identity is used to organize task losses and gradient observations, but is not supplied to the head or router. Both the trainable representation and the router can learn task differences from the inputs; expert mixing is one component of this adaptation.

Sharing output weights aliases task-local label indices with different semantics or polarity, creating competition in the shared prediction space. In three-logit mixtures, all three classes participate in softmax and prediction for binary examples as well. Every compared method uses this same shared-output convention.

The alignment pathway is the one of Section 5 with the routed unit being a same-task example group: gmg_{m} sums the group-loss gradients across experts in the common LoRA parameter template and is detached as g~m=stopgrad⁡(gm)\tilde{g}_{m}=\mathrm{stopgrad}(g_{m}) for the auxiliary loss. From detached pooled representations stopgrad⁡(hn)\mathrm{stopgrad}(h_{n}), the auxiliary branch recomputes per-example router probabilities qnq_{n} using top-4 masked softmax over eight experts. It then sets pm=|m|−1​∑n∈mqnp_{m}=|m|^{-1}\sum_{n\in m}q_{n}, with no further top-kk operation on the group mean. Thus pmp_{m} can have more than kk nonzero entries even when each example selects only kk experts. The ℒnorm\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{norm}} objective with ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8} has no direct gradient to non-router parameters; detaching hnh_{n} preserves its derivatives with respect to router parameters while blocking this branch from the backbone. Groups contain eight examples; the per-task batch schedule and the five seeds used throughout match the frozen LoRA-FFN setting, and final runs use 2,000 updates. The final optimizer and method-specific values are reported in Tables 13 and 14.

D.6 Trainable RoBERTa Classification-Head Top-1

This comparison keeps the trainable classification-head setting of Appendix D.5 unchanged, namely the fully trainable RoBERTa-base backbone, the rank-16 LoRA experts over the shared base head, the shared output width, and the linear router on the masked-mean pooled representation, and replaces the top-4 masked-softmax gate by the straight-through one-hot gate of Appendix D.4 applied to the per-example router logits (E8K1). Each example is therefore dispatched to one expert in the forward computation, while the backward derivative is the full-softmax Jacobian. GAR recomputes the same gate from the detached pooled representation, averages it over the eight examples of each same-task group, and pairs the group probability with the detached expert-gradient observation as in Section 5; task losses are weighted as in Appendix D.10. This comparison includes Baseline, CAGrad, and GAR.

The batch schedule, update budget, and selection protocol are those of the top-4 classification-head comparison: per-task batch size 32 with same-task groups of eight, 2,000 optimizer updates, five shared final seeds, and the Baseline-first search of Appendix D.2. Baseline searches its learning rate, clipping, and weight decay; CAGrad and GAR inherit the selected clipping and weight decay and search their own learning rate and coefficient (cc and λalign\lambda_{\mathrm{align}}, respectively), with CAGrad’s inner learning rate fixed at 0.10.1. Table 15 lists the selected learning rates, the shared clipping and weight decay, and the selected coefficients.

D.7 Trainable DeBERTa Full-Parameter FFN MoE

This setting retains the expert insertion sites and token-level routing of the frozen LoRA-FFN comparison while changing the expert parameterization and backbone trainability. The microsoft/deberta-v3-base backbone is fully trainable, and each expert is a complete feed-forward block at the final-layer feed-forward insertion sites, without LoRA factorization, so the routed unit is a token rather than a pooled sequence. All five mixtures use top-4 routing over eight experts (E8K4) at sequence length 256, matching the frozen LoRA-FFN setting. This extension also retains a separate prediction head with the appropriate output width for each task. All computation is FP32. The alignment pathway, the detached gradient observations, and the ℒnorm\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{norm}} objective are those of Section 5, with the same-task example groups formed at the micro-batch sizes recorded in Table 16. This setting compares Baseline, CAGrad, and GAR.

The three methods use the shared batch schedule and a 2,000-update budget. Baseline first selects learning rate, clipping, and weight decay using Appendix D.2’s procedure. Subsequent methods inherit the selected clipping and weight decay and tune their own learning rates and applicable coefficients. Warmup is fixed at 0.10.1. The following table gives the configurations.

D.8 DeBERTa Single-Task Configurations

Both DeBERTa single-task adaptations use four experts with top-2 routing (E4K2). The LoRA variant uses the frozen-backbone LoRA architecture described in Appendix D.2. The FFN variant unfreezes the backbone and uses full-parameter FFN experts at the same final-layer insertion sites, without a LoRA factorization. The router, expert parameters, and classification head are trainable in both variants; backbone parameters are also trainable in the FFN variant. These architectural choices are shared by Baseline, CAGrad, and GAR.

Within each adaptation, the compared methods use the same experimental protocol. For each task and adaptation, Baseline first selects learning rate, clipping, and weight decay using Appendix D.2’s procedure. Subsequent methods inherit the selected clipping and weight decay and tune their own learning rates and applicable coefficients. Warmup is fixed at 0.10.1. All runs use sequence length 128, effective batch size 16, and same-task groups of eight examples. These sizes were selected by the same DeBERTa CAGrad development-probe procedure, applied to MRPC, and are reused for all five tasks, both adaptations, and all three methods; as in the multi-task settings, only the batch sizes are transferred, not CAGrad’s learning rate or coefficients. SST-2 and QQP use 3 epochs; CoLA, MRPC, and RTE use 5 epochs. Tables 17 and 18 list the LoRA and FFN configurations, respectively.

D.9 RoBERTa Fixed-Configuration Coefficient Ablations

We report separate RoBERTa LoRA-FFN and classification-head LoRA coefficient sweeps on the same five E8K4 dataset mixtures listed in Tables 19 and 20. For each setting and mixture, we reuse the corresponding selected GAR configuration, including learning rate, gradient clipping, weight decay, batch and micro-batch sizes, sequence length, warmup ratio, expert topology, backbone trainability, and numerical precision. The training budget is reduced from 2,000 to 1,000 updates for every coefficient, with the same five random seeds shared across coefficients. Within each sweep, only λ∈{0,10−5,10−4,10−3,10−2}\lambda\in\{0,10^{-5},10^{-4},10^{-3},10^{-2}\} varies; no additional HPO or per-coefficient configuration selection is performed. Both settings use the common-template gradient observations defined in Section 3.3. At λ=0\lambda=0, the auxiliary backward pass is disabled. This task-loss-only control retains the matched GAR configuration and is distinct from the separately tuned Baseline in the main comparison.
